Models, Theory, and Research Strategies: Toward the Evolution of New Paradigms

Robert Langs MD

Robert Langs

16th Street and First Avenue
New York, NY 10003

Robert Langs  

This paper will describe how the communicative approach to psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic psychotherapy has become an investigative research strategy — not only a valid basis for quantitative characterization of moment-to-moment transactions in the therapeutic context, but a means of understanding the principles by which we, in the broadest sense, process and adapt to emotionally changed information. The communicative approach is very much an outgrowth of psychoanalysis and has evolved by means of its emphasis on one particular dimension of psychoanalytic theory. But the approach has also been derived from my own clinical experience and ideas, so its history is entwined with my own. This paper will therefore reflect aspects of both personal and professional evolution. I intend to chart the development of the communicative approach from the first clinical paper written from that particular view point (Langs, 1971) to its present function as an instrument of investigative research.

My working assumption as a communicative therapist is that the moment-to-moment transactions between therapist and patient take place within a field whose parameters are concrete and essentially structure the kind of dyad possible.

Dr. Langs is Chief, Center for Communicative Research, Beth Israel Medical Center.

[[RunningHead]]

Philosophy, Psychoanalysis, and the Problem of Change

Volney Gay PHD

Volney Gay

Nashville, TN 37235

Volney Gay  

My argument in brief is that psychoanalysts rarely espouse metaphysical opinions. Hence to contrast an analytic philosophy of change with its competitors, one must first uncover metaphysical opinions that are only implicit in psychoanalytic writings. In this paper I do just that. Freud's basic theory of cure, I suggest, is best seen as a variation on the theme of mourning stated in his essay, “Mourning and Melancholia” (1917). There we learn that change and object loss are permanent features of human experience. Indeed, without object loss there can be no maturation. The philosophic corollary of this clinical claim is that philosophers who deny the reality of object loss thereby frustrate mourning, and they therefore inhibit the possibility of full human development. To make this point clear I contrast Freud's valuation of mourning with two metaphysical competitors: ancient religious beliefs and Christian religious beliefs. Finally, I argue that Freud's basic metaphysical concerns reappear in clinical discussions of the goals of analysis, where we find represented analytic values, which, in turn, stem from his unswerving opposition to religious promises of transformation.

Professor Gay is Associate Professor of Religious Studies and Associate Professor of Psychiatry, Vanderbilt University; Senior Clinical Candidate, St. Louis Psychoanalytic Institute.

[[RunningHead]]

Epilogue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

Three themes are repeated in the preceding essays: (1) Psychoanalytic data are unique to the psychoanalytic situation; (2) research designs can be developed to test data and verify psychoanalytic theory; (3) the canons of modern science which address the criteria for scientific activity, the falsification by empirical evidence (Popper, 1968) and eliminative inductivism (Grünbaum, 1984) apply to psychoanalysis. The critics of psychoanalysis as a valid scientific activity can be seriously debated.

Psychoanalysis is at a junction where improved communication is necessary with the scientific and nonscientific communities. Further development of psychoanalytic research methodology is an important component in our capacity to communicate. Unless psychoanalysts are able to communicate in a language that is consonant with the scientific community regarding psychoanalytic activity, psychoanalysis will be unable to respond creatively to the demands and changes within modern science. Moreover, unless psychoanalysts are able to communicate effectively about the efficacy of psychoanalysis with the nonscientific community, psychoanalysis will be relegated to the position of being considered an unimportant and ineffective oddity in current health-delivery programs.

The Sea Worms: A Case of Arrested Development

Mary Newsome MD

Mary Newsome

180 N. Michigan Blvd. Suite 2316
Chicago, IL 60601

Mary Newsome  

It is the purpose of this paper to describe the course of a psychoanalytic treatment of a woman who suffered a developmental arrest in her second year of life. Her transference experiences will be correlated with concepts derived from developmental psychology, learning theory, and communication science. A brief description of the theoretical orientation informing my work follows:

I follow Kohut (1984) in subscribing to the fundamental importance of a reliable organization of the self, understood as a structure functioning as a center of initiative, receiving its unique stamp from the constellation of ambitions and ideals it embodies. I follow Basch (1973, 1974, 1976a, 1977, 1981, 1983) in his description of the origin of the self in an open system developing between mother and baby, mediated initially by their visual interactions. The affect-laden sensorimotor patterns the infant develops in the presymbolic period are gradually unified into an enduring structure during the second year of life when the capacity to symbolize permits the child to objectify his experience. Repression may be said to occur when sensorimotor experiences do not achieve symbolization, for logical operations cannot be performed on what has not been given symbolic representation.

Dr. Newsome is on the Faculty of the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis; she is Associate at Northwestern University, Department of Psychiatry.

Epilogue

Estelle Shane Issue Editor and Morton Shane Issue Editor

Morton Shane

Morton Shane  

As is evident, there is considerable variation in the theoretical orientation and focus of interest among the contributors to this issue, but each is in agreement concerning the necessity to conceptualize the role of development in psychoanalytic theory and practice. It would seem appropriate, then, to conclude with some comments about the place of development in the history of the field.

Historically, development has been so integral to psychoanalysis that when Rapaport and (Gill, in 1959, attempted their formulations of the definitive points of view in metapsychology they seriously considered not delineating a separate developmental point of view at all, it seemed so pervasive. From one perspective, therefore, psychoanalytic development is psychoanalysis. For example, the concept of the sequence of libidinal phases, their progressions, regressions, and fixations, was for a very long time viewed as almost synonymous with analytic thought. Over time, additional developmental concepts were integrated into the central paradigm, including the progression from pleasure principle to reality principle, development of the ego, and formation and maturation of the superego. Lines of development of object relations and self and their indigitation are more recent additions to the body of psychoanalytic thought. Moreover, adult development has gained increasing recognition as a useful concept. In sum then, the history of its developmental theory is remarkably close to a history of psychoanalysis per se. This may explain why these papers incorporate such diversity, yet display a unity of the theme.

Prologue

Donald Ross Issue Editor

Donald Ross

Donald Ross  

When, on April 4, 1988, Sheppard Pratt Hospital opened its new Education Center, the occasion was celebrated with the hospital's 25th annual Scientific Day program. The theme for this program, “Psychoanalytic Perspectives on the Borderline Patient,” was of great interest to the hospital and the psychoanalytic community of Baltimore and Washington. Jacob Arlow, Clarence Schulz, Arnold Goldberg, and Joseph Lichtenberg were invited to discuss, from their different psychoanalytic viewpoints, the case of a borderline patient who had been treated for a year as an inpatient on our Personality Disorder Treatment and Research Unit.

The patient's therapist, Susan Pearson, opened the program by presenting the case. This was followed by individual discussions of the case by Drs. Arlow, Schulz, and Goldberg, representing the classical, object relational, and self psychological perspectives. Dr. Lichtenberg then formally contrasted these viewpoints and added his own discussion of the case based on his theory of motivational systems. The program ended with a panel discussion and open dialogue with the audience in which these four viewpoints were compared and contrasted. This was such a rich and stimulating day that we subsequently asked Harold Searles (who was present in the audience), Murray Jackson (from the Kleinian school), and Ernest Wolf (a preeminent interpreter of self psychology) to add discussions on the case from their perspectives.

We believe this report of our program captures the spirit of inquiry and creative thinking that was so apparent at this inaugural conference for the Education Center.

Baltimore MD 21204

Susan Pearson  

THEY BUILT A HOUSE

OF VELVET BRICKS

EACH ONE PRESOAKED

IN BLOOD.

WHEN THEY TAPPED

THEM INTO PLACE

THE RED SPEW

CAUSED A FLOOD.

These are the words of a poem Mrs. X wrote shortly after her admission to The Sheppard and Enoch Pratt Hospital in the summer of 1986. The words described her feelings and fears about what hospitalization would mean to her, her fears of change, of healing, and the cost.

This was her first hospitalization, though she had been in psychotherapy for ten years. Her chief complaint upon admission was, “My therapist insisted that I come into the hospital to work on our relationship.”

Mrs. X is 50-years old, married, the mother of two teenage children. She has a masters degree and is an award-winning teacher at a prestigious private school in a large city.

Discussion: Self Psychology and Mrs. X.

Ernest Wolf MD

Ernest Wolf

1333 Tower Road
Winnetka, IL 60093

Ernest Wolf  

The psychoanalyst as discussant of another therapist's case report finds himself in an odd position. He is expected to come up with brilliant new insights that the treating therapist failed to mention. If he is identified with some particular point of view among the mainstreams of psychoanalytic theory he is expected to convincingly demonstrate, or at least attempt to demonstrate, the superiority of his way of looking at data. He is supposed to achieve these herculean feats of psychoanalytic understanding without having access to any truly psychoanalytic data, for he is wholly dependent on somebody else's reports of what that other analytic therapist took to be data.

By definition, true psychoanalytic data are not publicly observable since they are made up of the private experiences of both analyst and analysand. Being thus dependent on the treating therapist's choices in reporting the treatment — choices that are dictated both by theory and by willingness to suffer the pains of self-disclosure — the discussant is necessarily limited to what are, at best, educated guesses. Sometimes these conjectures may be very close to what he might have concluded had he been the treating analyst; sometimes his speculations are far off the mark of what actually happened in the therapeutic enterprise being reported.

Dr. Wolf is a Training and Supervising Analyst at the Chicago Institute for Psychoanalysis; he is also Assistant Professor of Psychiatry at Northwestern University Medical School.

I have found that after i have presented on a topic such as we are considering today some members of the audience invariably ask, “What has this approach of long-term treatment for these patients to do with our limitation of 21 days of hospitalization?” My remarks have been dismissed as impractical and suited only to an ivory-tower treatment situation. There are, of course, several valid treatment approaches with borderline patients. These could include behavior modification, cognitive therapy, medications, brief psychotherapy, supportive therapy, analysis, environmental manipulation, and even antihospitalization, to list a few.

Discussion: A Kleinian Perspective

Murray Jackson FRCP, FRCPsych.

Murray Jackson

67 Princes Way
London SW 19 6 HZ
England

Murray Jackson  

The spectrum of patients currently liable to be classified as Borderline is so wide that much energy has been spent in recent years in the attempt to refine the concept and to establish satisfactory defining criteria (Grinker et al., 1968; Jackson & Pines, 1986a; Frosch, 1988; Jackson & Tarnopolsky, 1989). One recurring theme of dispute concerns the justifiability of including a susceptibility to brief or “micropsychotic” episodes as an essential diagnostic requirement. This theme has special significance when one addresses the question of the nature of the profound developmental arrest that is generally agreed to lie at the core of this disorder. Some clinicians would wish the diagnosis of borderline to be abandoned, holding that despite all efforts to refine the category, it remains too vague and diffuse. Frosch (1988), in particular, regards the neurotic content as the expression of underlying psychotic mechanisms and argues that the term should be abandoned and replaced by his concept of “psychotic character.”

Klein's formulation of the paranoid-schizoid position concerned this very issue, the nature and sequence of primitive developmental processes in the infant and small child and the way they underlie subsequent neurotic pathology and predispose to later psychotic developments (Klein, 1946; see also Spillius, 1988).

Murray Jackson FRCP, FRCPsych, is Emeritus Consultant Psychiatrist and Psychotherapist, Maudsley Hospital and Kings College Hospital, London.

Epilogue

Donald Ross Issue Editor

Donald Ross

Donald Ross  

The study of borderline patients has become one of the most important arenas for the advancement of psychoanalytic knowledge. It has focused renewed attention on preoedipal drive development (especially aggression), the formation of early object relationships, the development of a unified self, and the vicissitudes of narcissistic libido. The techniques of psychoanalysis and psychoanalytically informed psychotherapy have been expanded by our need to accommodate to the needs of these more disturbed patients. The concepts of parameter, holding environment, transitional phenomena, and therapeutic milieu have evolved from the analytic work with borderline and psychotic individuals. The scope of our understanding and our technical expertise have indeed widened, and this has enriched our field.

The opportunity to work with seriously ill patients in a hospital setting over an extended period of time is an invaluable training experience. At Sheppard Pratt, we require our psychiatric residents-in-training to spend one year on the long-term inpatient services. Expert supervision is clearly instrumental in the successful use of this setting for training. Some of the more difficult and important lessons can be learned here best. Transference and countertransference passions come to life with dramatic intensity. Projective identification and splitting become tangible processes. The concept of the treatment team and the roles of therapist and team leader are brought into high relief, requiring careful definition. In such a crucible, one's identity as a psychoanalytically oriented therapist may be born and reborn.

Joseph Lichtenberg  

In 1912, at the age of 24, eugene o'neill sensed a great change in himself. To quote one biographer, “He found that, without conscious effort, story ideas, scraps of plot and dramatic situations—peopled largely by seamen, prostitutes, other battered souls—were welling up and crowding his thoughts. He continued to work on poems but also began to record his story ideas, expanding some into detailed outlines” (Sheaffer, 1968, p. 225). It was at this point in his life that he was determined to form and realize his ambition to be a creative writer. He expressed his aim in terms of unmistakeable competition and grandiosity: “Some day James O'Neill will best be known as the father of Eugene O'Neill” (Sheaffer, 1968, p. 225). He was preparing to take on his famous actor father as rival, and to challenge him in the arena of his success—the theater. Four years later his identity as a developing creative artist was realized.

When we think of Eugene O'Neill, we think of a playwright, himself tormented, who created a theater peopled by characters deeply in conflict with one another and with society—an American counterpart to Strindberg and Ibsen. I am addressing myself here to the subject of a younger O'Neill. I am exploring the inner world of the creative writer-to-be during adolescence and its prolongation into the early adult years (Erikson, 1959).

Theories evolving from different hypotheses provide plausible convincing but contradictory explanations for the same clinical data. This phenomena is both blessing and curse: blessing because it demonstrates the vitality and complexity of the human condition and our creative imaginations in conceptualizing it; curse because of the confusion and uncertainty we must live with as we listen and learn. We have just had the opportunity to consider five expositions of Pearson's case report of Mrs. X and her treatment by leaders in our field. Prologue

Melvin Bornstein Issue Editor

Melvin Bornstein

Melvin Bornstein  

This issue of psychoanalytic inquiry is devoted to the methodology of psychoanalytic research. Together the papers illuminate some of the most vital issues confronting contemporary psychoanalysis: the relationship of psychoanalysis to modern science, the efficacy of psychoanalytic practice, and the continued development of psychoanalysis as a viable theory and treatment modality.

Three-quarters of a century ago Freud set forth the relationship between treatment and research as an inseparable bond. “In psycho-analysis there has existed from the very first an inseparable bond between cure and research. Knowledge brought therapeutic success. It was impossible to treat a patient without learning something new; it was impossible to gain fresh insight without perceiving its beneficial results. Our analytic procedure is the only one in which this precious conjunction is assured. It is only by carrying on our analytic pastoral work that we can deepen our dawning comprehension on the human mind. This prospect of scientific gain has been the proudest and happiest feature of analytic work (1927, p. 256).

Freud argued that the methodology of psychoanalytic research is identical to that of the physical sciences. At that time the canons of science were based upon logical positivism—the investigation of a fixed external reality devoid of subjective experience that could be completely understood. Because of the narrowness of logical positivism, it was impossible to develop a methodology for psychoanalytic research compatible with the physical sciences.

Henry Bachrach

903 Park Avenue

Henry Bachrach  

In speaking of a new romance during the second year of her analysis, an analysand who had originally sought treatment shortly after the untimely loss of her mother remarked that “passion is pain's pawn.” She paused as she was taken by the gripping but uncertain meaning of her thought. She went on to say that the close proximity between her mother's loss and the ending of her first romantic adventure somehow seemed connected. Her thoughts then turned to the guilt she felt when she left home for school, which she connected to her original thought — “passion is pain's pawn” — and then back to reminiscenses of conflicts with her mother and the pain she felt at her mother's loss. At this point I remarked she seemed to be thinking about the pain associated with her romantic involvements and her mother's loss at the same time, that there was a contiguity in her associations.

“I knew you were going to say that”, she said with irritation. It sounded textbookish to her. I recognized my observation had stirred her, it was that she preferred I not categorize her with what she saw as easy formulas. She felt her original thought had more meaning when she put it in her own way, and went on with this line of thinking. At the close of the hour I suggested the way I had put my observation had made her feel “less special.

The Idealization of Structural Change

David Werman MD

David Werman

Durham, NC 27710

David Werman  

Akeystone of psychoanalytic teaching over the past four or five decades has been the concept that the principal goal and optimal achievement of “successful” psychoanalysis is a change in “psychic structure,” brought about by the “resolution” of the analysand's infantile and childhood neuroses and conflicts. This formulation has characteristically stressed the contrast between structural changes and the more limited goals and achievements of psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy, wherein only some modification of derivative aspects of the deepest neurotic conflicts is sought, while the “core” conflicts themselves are permitted to remain intact. Even though a patient in psychotherapy may have achieved marked changes in “derivative” behavior, this traditional formulation asserts that the patient is deemed to be vulnerable to subsequent neurotic difficulties.

Most analysts who advance this point of view hasten to add that they do not believe psychoanalytically oriented psychotherapy is an inferior treatment, compared to psychoanalysis, but that it is merely a different form of therapy, usually with different indications, different goals, and, to some extent, different techniques. That psychoanalysis is described as “going deeper,” having a greater prophylactic power, more “enduring,” able to modify the “roots” (core conflicts) of a disorder and not only its “branches” (symptoms, etc.)

The Common Core of Paranoia and Depression

H. Bloch MD

H. Bloch

706 D Street
San Rafael, CA 94901

H. Bloch  

This is a study of patients who proved to be concomitantly paranoid and depressed, even though some of them had not sought treatment for either of these conditions. The existence of their paranoia and depression was often first identified in their transference, after the treatment seemed to have reached a stalemate. It turned out that the patients had mistrusted my motives to help them. And they had hidden this mistrust from me and from themselves because they felt guilty about mistrusting me. Therapeutic efforts to relieve their guilt over mistrusting me were gradually followed by reduction of their paranoia and depression and by progression in treatment.

From what proved to be very long but successful analyses (without parameters) and therapies, I arrived at the following paradigm for development in these patients: At some period during their childhood, they had experienced a seemingly insoluble developmental conflict. They had perceived that what was required to please their parents was stifling certain of their own strivings toward maturity.

Dr. Bloch is a practicing psychoanalyst of children, adolescents, and adults.

Jacob Arlow MD

Jacob Arlow

120 East 36th Street
New York, NY 10016

Jacob Arlow  

Many, many years ago, before there was radio or television, the authentic rite of passage into the outer world consisted of receiving your first library card. On that auspicious day, I knew exactly what I would do—the same as my older friends had done. And so I rushed to the library and took out the Red Fairy Book. By the end of the week, I had been through the Red, the Green, the Yellow, and the Blue Fairy Books.

It did not take long to recognize a familiar, repetitive theme that ran through so many of the stories. It concerned three brothers who were charged by the king to solve a difficult problem or bring back some magic talisman. The successful brother was awarded the hand of the beautiful princess in marriage and was next in line to ascend the throne. The results were always predictable. The oldest brother, a practical but unimaginative dolt, returned first. He had the wrong answer. He was given short shrift and then faded completely from the picture. The middle brother fared somewhat better, but not much. The youngest brother, however, was always the successful one—not at all, mind you, by virtue of his native ability but in consequence of some act of kindness from which he became the beneficiary of magical intervention by a toad, a gnome, a genie, or a fairy godmother in disguise.

I found this scenario most appealing.

Some time ago a patient remarked about his irritation with the solicitations of a friend who, because the patient was ill, in bed, called him three times during a 24-hour period to see how he was doing, waking him up with each and every phone call. The patient was grumbling about how people aren't really concerned about others so much as they are anxious about themselves, that it is only their own problems that lead them to be solicitous of others. Concepts of Therapeutic Effectiveness in Psychoanalysis: A Historical Review

Arnold Cooper MD

Arnold Cooper

525 East 68th Street
New York, NY 10021

Arnold Cooper  

From the very inception of psychoanalysis in the work of Breuer and Freud, analysts have conjectured over how it is that analysis has its therapeutic effect. Why does it work? How does the analytic process bring about psychic change? The usual companion question—does it work—was not seriously addressed by Freud, nor, some would say, has it been addressed since. We will continue in that tradition, taking at face value the evidence of nearly a century of clinical experience that analysis does have therapeutic benefit, well aware of the hazards of equating clinical belief with scientific knowledge, and we will again ask how does analysis work.

Changes in our views on the sources of the therapeutic effectiveness of psychoanalysis have appropriately followed upon changes in psychoanalytic theory and our ideas of the nature of the analytic process. Clearly these changes have been profound and frequent, and a review such as this can only touch on a few major questions. The fullest discussion of the subject would involve us in the entire history of psychoanalytic thought. This review, therefore, will stress only a few high points.

Dr. Cooper is Professor of Psychiatry, Cornell University Medical College; Training and Supervising Analyst, Columbia University Psychoanalytic Center for Training and Research.

Structural and Interstructural Change in Psychoanalytic Treatment

Leo Rangell MD

Leo Rangell

456 N. Carmelina Avenue
Los Angeles, CA 90049

Leo Rangell  

“Structural change” has become an almost automatic phrase to differentiate psychoanalytic insight-producing therapy from supportive psychotherapies, which aim to strengthen an overburdened ego by the therapist supplying emotional support. Following psychotherapeutic support, the patient's ego returns to its premorbid state. If practical results accord with theoretical expectations, following the specific experience of the analytic treatment the ego advances to a new normal state. Clinical experiences and experimental research have been putting these theoretical formulations to the test for over half a century.

Structural change has become the accepted phrase, almost a symbol for analytic change. Curiously, it is used more widely than its meaning is known or established. And paradoxically, it has come into automatic usage even by psychotherapists who discard the theory of psychic structures or who operate without the concept of interstructural conflict. With such contradictions, the automatic use of the term has become an unexamined cliché.

Dr. Rangell is Past-President, American Psychoanalytic Association; Past-President, International Psychoanalytic Association; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, UCLA School of Medicine; Clinical Professor of Psychiatry (Psychoanalysis), University of California School of Medicine, San Francisco.

This contribution is a modified version of a paper read to a Conference on “How People Change. The Potential for Structural Change in Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy.” Sponsored by The Adolescent Day Treatment Center of the Psychiatric Service of Children's Hospital of San Francisco. A Reconstruction of Freud's Tally Argument: A Program for Psychoanalytic Research

Wilma Bucci PHD

Wilma Bucci

Garden City, NY 11530

Wilma Bucci  

In developing his scientific method, Freud attempted to reconcile oppositions—possibly without recognizing them as such; some of the problems in psychoanalytic theory and technique arise from this. The first opposition concerns the subject matter of the theory. Psychoanalytic propositions refer to private and subjective mental representations—expectations, feelings, beliefs—known directly only to their experiencers; known only partially even to them. However, the domain of science calls for mutually observable events. Freud was attempting to build a science out of subjective representations without confronting the epistemological difficulties inherent in that attempt.

The second opposition lies in Freud's intent of combining the roles of scientist and clinician, with all the different functions that each role entails. In any treatment situation the practitioner's primary responsibility is to help the patient. The scientist's commitment is to investigate the research questions wherever they may lead; this can diverge from, even interfere with the responsibility to treat. In the analytic situation, in which transference (and countertransference) play a central role, the difficulties inherent in the scientist-practitioner duality are even more acute.

Epilogue

Pietro Castelnuovo-Tedesco Issue Editor

Pietro Castelnuovo-Tedesco

Pietro Castelnuovo-Tedesco  

When one undertakes the review of a key psychoanalytic topic or concept one is struck by how complex the task invariably turns out to be. The amount of “unpacking” to be done—to borrow a phrase from Spence (1982)—is, to say the least, daunting; the meanings, shades of meanings, and possibilities that present themselves and need to be accounted for, just keep unrolling and seemingly go on and on. As with an individual analysis, the place where one decides to stop is in a sense arbitrary and a matter of convenience. One could certainly go further.

I had this sense very much in dealing with the topic under consideration here. The eight papers in this issue are rich and varied in content, yet in conclusion one can say that their number easily could have been doubled. Clearly, there is more that each author—ot other authors—would have chosen to say, given the opportunity. At the same time, it is remarkable how much consensus exists among the various contributors. We note differences in emphasis and some differences in terminology rather than outright disagreements.

Historically, as both Cooper and Meissner indicate, change has been a central concern of analysts since the beginning of the analytic enterprise. Initially, the focus was on symptom removal, although already by 1913 the notion of “transference cure” (Freud, 1913) as opposed to “true” analytic resolution, entered the literature. With the development of the structural theory (Freud, 1923, Hartmann, 1939), the emphasis on change as structural change became both clearer and dominant. As Werman points out, the focus also shifted from primarily clinical to primarily metapsychological considerations, although clinical changes have always been required for making metapsychological inferences.

A Note on Psychoanalytic Facts

W. Meissner SJ

W. Meissner

129 Mount Auburn Street
Cambridge MA 02138

W. Meissner  

In the last score of years, psychoanalysis has been caught up in a swirl of new theoretical options, prompted for the most part by dissatisfaction or uneasiness about the scientific status of the received metapsychology. Traditional theory had it that psychoanalysis was a natural science and therefore followed the methods and techniques of theory construction of a natural scientific methodology. The revolt against the natural-science model brought into question both the impersonal mechanistic quality of the natural-science account (Schafer, 1976) and the unscientific contamination of the account by metaphorical and anthropomorphized concepts (Grossman & Simon, 1969; Wurmser, 1977). Alternative theories substituted a view of psychoanalysis as a humanistic discipline, based on personal data that were impregnated with meaning and followed the model of various humanistic disciplines (Meissner, 1985). Thus psychoanalysis was seen as a linguistic discipline (Lacan, 1968, 1977; Ricoeur, 1970; Edelson, 1975), as a form of historical knowledge (Novey, 1968; Schafer, 1978, 1983; Wallace, 1985), or as a more specifically experiential or existential enterprise (Kohut, 1971, 1977). The emphasis on personal relationships and interpersonal influence of the object relations approach would bring it under the latter category (Greenberg & Mitchell, 1983).

The tensions in this debate may ultimately be irresolvable.

Dr. Meissner is Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Institute; University Professor of Psychoanalysis, Boston College, Chestnut Hill, MA.

The Therapeutic Action of Psychoanalysis: Strachey Revisited

W. Meissner S.J.

W. Meissner

129 Mount Auburn Street
Cambridge, MA 02138

W. Meissner  

The nature of change in psychoanalysis and the explanation for the effectiveness of psychoanalytic interventions has been one of the perennial problems in the understanding of the psychoanalytic process. Strachey's (1934) paper stands as the classical magisterial statement of the role of interpretation as the vehicle for change in psychoanalysis. In the half-century and more since Strachey's paper, the theoretical context, in which the understanding of the psychoanalytic process is achieved, has changed radically and has undergone significant evolution.

Strachey wrote within a theoretical context dominated by the revolutionary development of the structural theory (Freud, 1923) and the work on group psychology (Freud, 1921). The implications of the structural hypothesis, and particularly Freud's early structural formulations regarding the origin and functions of the ego and superego, had only begun to find their way into technical application. But this was also the period before the appearance of Anna Freud's work on the mechanisms of defense (1936) and Hartmann's revolutionary statement of the autonomous and adaptive capacities of the ego (1939), both of which were to have far-reaching effects on the technical evolution of psychoanalysis.

Dr. Meissner is Training and Supervising Analyst, Boston Psychoanalytic Institute; University Professor of Psychoanalysis, Boston College; formerly Clinical Professor of Psychiatry, Harvard Medical School.

Prologue

Pietro Castelnuovo-Tedesco Issue Editor

Pietro Castelnuovo-Tedesco

Pietro Castelnuovo-Tedesco  

The question of change and therapeutic effectiveness is at the heart of the therapeutic enterprise and has played a special role in the development of psychoanalysis and its close relative, psychoanalytic psychotherapy. Arguably, the issue of therapeutic effectiveness influences the present standing of psychoanalysis and psychoanalytic psychotherapy perhaps more than any other that might be raised. It is the sum and substance of the psychoanalytic undertaking.

Freud on various occasions (1913, 1914, 1923b, 1925, 1933, 1940) took pains to emphasize that psychoanalysis was much more than simply a form of treatment. He stressed the value of psychoanalysis as a method of scientific inquiry, as a general psychology of the mind, and as a cultural achievement; in the context of technique, he (1912, 1933) warned against therapeutic zeal. Nonetheless, for many the significance of psychoanalysis has been tied primarily to its therapeutic potential, to its capacity to bring relief to a broad range of emotional disorders, perhaps even to “cure” them.

Psychoanalysis has taken special pride in its power to bring about psychic change, and in fact this has been viewed as a special attribute of analytic therapy in comparison with and in contrast to other therapies. From the beginning, its qualifications as a “depth psychology” have meant that psychoanalysis sought to go deeper than the symptoms and their alleviation, that it sought to deal with the unconscious factors that underlie the neurosis and are responsible for its unfolding.

Therapeutic Change: Perspectives of Self Psychology

David Terman MD

David Terman

35 East Wacker Drive, Suite 3200
Chicago, IL 6060

David Terman  

For kohut, the stated central vehicle for structuralization and therapeutic change was the phenomenon he conceptualized as transmuting internalization. First introduced in 1971 (pp. 49-51), and resting solidly on Freud's theory of the work of mourning, it consisted of three steps: (1) a receptivity for introjects, (2) the “breaking up” of the aspects (psychological functions) of the object via optimal frustration and (3) the depersonalization of those aspects of the object and their transformation into an integral part of the patient's psychic structure. “The internal structure, in other words, now performs the functions which the object used to perform for the child—the well-functioning structure, however, has largely been divested of the personality features of the object” (p. 50).

The “breaking up” process derives from Freud's (1917) explanation of the mechanism of mourning. Estelle Shane Issue Editor and Morton Shane Issue Editor

Morton Shane

Morton Shane  

The papers to follow incorporate diverse theoretical perspectives and focus on different phases in the life cycle. But they share a common commitment to the importance of a developmental perspective. And while each of the authors puts forward his or her own ideas on this perspective, we would like to submit a short statement of our own. We take for granted that psychological development is lifelong, a stance derived initially from our experience as child analysts and then extrapolated to our work with adult patients. For as child analysts working with children in distress we had become accustomed to viewing symptomatology not as a fixed formation but rather as a dynamic entity superimposed upon and related to an underlying, ongoing development process. The process itself is often hampered and skewed; yet it is surprisingly persistent. Analytic experience with adults has revealed to us the usefulness of conceptualizing a similar and still powerful ongoing psychological developmental process in adulthood. This position is in distinct contrast to the view of adulthood as a mature, nondevelopmental state. In this latter view, one completes psychological growth at some designated time, usually with the offset of adolescence, unless development has been impeded earlier by psychotic, neurotic, or character problems.

This dichtomy between the view of psychological development as lifelong versus the view of psychological development as ending at maturity, however maturity is demarcated, inevitably influences one's vision of the analytic process in general.

Gil Noam PHD and Robert Kegan PHD

Robert Kegan

Oaks 4

Robert Kegan  

Psychoanalytic psychology — underlying much of mental health practice — and Piagetian psychology — greatly influencing academic developmental psychology — have separate theoretical traditions, research orientations, and methods of intervention. Although both share developmental points of view, the differences are profound. One is a framework focusing on psychopathology, unconscious processes, and affective development; the other, a cognitive theory addressing structural reorganization in human thought.

These differences have contributed to past separation of the two fields. Interestingly, Freud and Piaget knew about each other's work as early as 1922 when Piaget presented his ideas about symbolic thought in Freud's presence. Since then, Piaget called repeatedly for a general psychology that could integrate psychoanalysis and the approach he termed genetic epistemology (Piaget, 1973). Despite this call, these two great developmental paradigms have had relatively little impact upon each other.

This paper, which I have had the pleasure of not only reading but of hearing presented by the author herself, is so excellent that it would be easy, and in many ways justified, for me to spend my allotted journal pages in expressions of admiration of Dr. Pearson, of her treatment of Mrs. X, and of her narrative of the patient's treatment.

I admire her ability to appreciate the creativity and the intendedly constructive potentiality — the healthy potential — of Mrs. X's symptoms, as when Pearson reports that “We looked in detail at the many functions that self-mutilation had served for her. It was a magical way to protect her children and the therapist from harm …. and was a way to define herself, to prove that she was real.”

I admire, too, Pearson's having so strong a self-esteem, so deep a sureness of her own worth, that she can freely acknowledge the contributions of other persons to Mrs. X's recovery — the contributions of, for example, the social worker, the patient's husband, and the art therapist. When she writes that “Mrs. X first allowed us a glimpse into her pathological side through her art work,” we sense that Pearson realizes that the series of the patient's paintings are more than merely signposts marking the progress which the patient is making in individual psychotherapy with the author herself, but are creative productions in the making of which the patient found innately therapeutic value.
